questions.q: In the visual conventions this lesson describes, what does an arrow in a lineage diagram represent?
options: The number of rows in a table
The physical distance between two servers
The seniority of the dataset's owner
The direction of data flow, from upstream to downstream
questions.explain: Arrows point from upstream to downstream, the same convention used in text form throughout this chapter since Lesson 12.

questions.q: What does a label placed directly on a lineage diagram's arrow typically represent?
options: The name of the diagram's author
A random identifier with no defined meaning
The transformation or business rule applied at that hop
The file size of the upstream dataset
questions.explain: An arrow label is where Lesson 13's business-rule logic becomes visible on the diagram itself, instead of staying buried in a separate document.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is a lineage diagram's relationship to the documentation from Lesson 17?
options: It completely replaces the need for any written documentation
It is unrelated and built from different information entirely
It only applies to automated lineage tools, never manual documentation
It's a visual view into that same underlying nodes-edges-ownership structure, not a separate source of truth
questions.explain: The diagram is how a human reads the documented graph at a glance; it's generated from, or kept consistent with, the same underlying structure.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend matching the level of detail in a diagram to its audience?
options: Because only engineers are ever shown lineage diagrams
Because regulations require a separate diagram for every job title
Because diagrams automatically simplify themselves for different audiences
Because one diagram dense enough for an engineer is usually too dense for an executive overview, and vice versa
questions.explain: An executive sign-off audience needs a handful of major systems with no column detail, while an engineer making a change needs every affected table and column — one diagram rarely serves both well.

questions.q: In the worked SourceTable -> StagingView -> FactTable -> Report diagram example, where would the Discount business rule from Lesson 13 be shown?
options: As a separate, unconnected box floating beside the diagram
Inside the SourceTable box only
As a label on the arrow for the specific hop where that transformation happens
It would not appear on the diagram at all
questions.explain: The lesson places the business rule directly on the arrow for the hop where it's applied, making the logic visible right where the transformation happens.
